articleTitle: 100 years of the Runge-Kutta method: a brief editing for schools
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This paper reports on the historical development of the Runge-Kutta methods beginning with the simple Euler method up to an embedded 13-stage method. Moreover, the design and the use of those methods under error order, stability and computation time conditions is edited for students of numerical analysis at undergraduate level. The second part presents applications in natural sciences, compares different methods and illustrates some of the difficulties of numerical solutions.

articleTitle: Mathematical Modelling and New Theories of Learning
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This article demonstrates the importance of expanding notions of learning beyond knowledge to the practices of mathematics classrooms. A three year study of students who learned through mathematical modelling is considered. This shows that a modelling approach encouraged the development of a range of important practices, in addition to knowledge, that were useful in real world situations.

articleTitle: Great theorems on a small screen
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: University of Gdansk third year undergraduates take a course called 'Elementary Number Theory'. During the course we try to introduce some important problems such as The Circle Problem, Dirichlet's Divisor Problem, Prime Number Theorem (PNT) or Fermat's Last Theorem. Working with graphing calculators students can experiment with these theorems. Obviously during the course we do not prove Fermat's Last Theorem, but we use the visualizing power of calculators such as TI92 Plus to help our students understand advanced mathematics better.

articleTitle: The crisis in Further Mathematics and how MEI and Gatsby are working to address it
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The number of students studying for A and AS level Further Mathematics has fallen dramatically since the early 1980s. Curriculum 2000 seems likely to worsen the situation. This article explains the decline and why it is vital that Further Mathematics is saved. Further Mathematics is needed to prepare students adequately for numerate degree courses; the single Mathematics A level does not achieve this. The second part of the article outlines the Gatsby‐funded MEI project ‘Enabling Access to Further Mathematics’, which aims to show that distance‐learning using modern technology can provide a viable solution to the problem of access to Further Mathematics.

articleTitle: The impact of school‐based assessment on the implementation of a modelling/applications‐based curriculum: an Australian example
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The impact of a school based assessment system on the implementation of an applications/modelling based curriculum at the senior secondary level is examined. In formal examination conditions, context‐separable and standard applications were common. In unsupervised, extended time conditions, tasks with low scaffolding allowed students to generate their own modelling solutions, whereas tasks high in scaffolding had the modelling structure already supplied by the task setter. The persistence of high task scaffolding in assessment tasks throughout the course, and the concerns of teachers about the reliability and ownership of assessment in unsupervised conditions, appeared to be restricting opportunities for students in some schools to demonstrate their modelling competencies.

articleTitle: Stopping distances: an excellent example of empirical modelling
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: In this paper we explore the derivation of empirical models for the stopping distance of a car being driven at a range of speeds. The calculation of stopping distances makes an excellent example of empirical modelling because it is a situation which is readily understood (and particularly relevant to many first year undergraduates who are learning or have just learnt to drive). Furthermore, there is easily accessible data and once simple empirical models have been developed it is possible to offer a physical justification of the models using only A level standard mechanics. US data on stopping distances illustrate the usefulness of looking at the overall behaviour of the error to determine limitations of the simple empirical model and the need to improve the fitting function. The need for an extra term in the improved empirical model gives insight into the reality of the physical situation.

articleTitle: An investigation of student working styles in a mathematical modelling activity
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: Four groups of mathematics undergraduates were observed carrying out a mathematical modelling exercise of a familiar physical process (cooling of a cup of hot water). We found that students neither took time to reflect upon the physical process nor to reflect on the appropriateness of the model they produced. They also appeared to be much more prone to take an empirical approach to modelling. We recommend that classroom instruction should promote this reflection, to encourage a theoretical approach, that data logging equipment should not be available at the outset and that students should be encouraged to discuss and explore the physical situation.

articleTitle: Maths woodwork it out
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: A practical woodwork problem is posed in which it is required to maximise the perimeter of a square‐based pyramid. The pyramid is constructed from four identical trapezia which are to be cut from a given rectangle of wood. A simple mathematical analysis suggests a number of different strategies for the solution of the problem.

articleTitle: The impact of dynamic geometry software on learning
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: I am undertaking research this year as part of a DFEE Best Practice Research Scholarship. This is ‘action research’ and is therefore based in school practice. It is focused on the use of the Internet to deliver resources direct to the secondary school teacher, which can be used in the teaching of geometry and which requires the minimum of learning on the teacher's part. My research considers the credibility, richness and value of such resources. This summary describes the setting up of the project, the data gathering and summary of data collected.My research question:The purpose of my research is to evaluate the credibility, richness and value of online learning using dynamic geometry.

articleTitle: APs, GPs and vCJD
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: When modelling the growth of any quantity the two simplest models assume either constant growth (where the same amount of new material is added in every time period) or proportionate growth (where the amount of new material in a time period is proportionate to the amount of material already present). For discrete models these growth assumptions lead to, respectively, arithmetic progressions and geometric progressions. The analysis of these sequences is accessible to A level students. It is also a very simple matter to implement such models within a spreadsheet. This allows easy investigation of the models and their sensitivity to parameter values. In this paper we describe an investigation of the applicability of these models to the onset on vCJD in humans. One of the important features of this investigation is that it demonstrates how simple mathematical techniques can sometimes allow a surprisingly robust qualitative conclusion to be drawn using sparse initial data. Given the restricted mathematical techniques required, this makes a powerful introduction to the use of mathematical models, which can be studied during the first week of an undergraduate career.

articleTitle: Rolling and spinning coin: a level gyroscopic processional motion
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This paper presents an example of precessional motion in mathematical terms available to students studying Further Pure and/or Further Mechanics A level mathematics. It shows how a real life example can be easily demonstrated. The mathematical solution helps students to see the applications of their Pure mathematics studies and gives a practical method to calculate the coefficient of friction of any surface.

articleTitle: A catenary problem
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: In this paper we develop a simple model to determine how high a static swing, with an occupant, is above the ground. The height of the swing is determined by how the supporting chains arrange themselves. Numerical solutions for several cases are calculated and these demonstrate that even though the shape of the supporting chains appears to vary considerably when they support differing weights, the actual effect on the height is minimal. We then go on to answer the question as to whether the same swing on the moon (carrying the same mass) sits higher or lower than the equivalent swing on earth.

articleTitle: Investigations into students' learning of applications in computer‐based learning environments
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: Based on a paradigmatic case study of a classroom situation in which students deal with functions within a computer‐aided learning environment, problems of modelling and application are investigated. In this connection two characteristic aspects of dealing with functions on object level are distinguished, namely a manipulative and a reflective approach, which have a provable impact on the students' ability of working with functions. The analysis of the case study shows that computer supported operating with functions as objects does not automatically lead to a better understanding of the function concept; if the manipulative approach dominates the reflective one, the features on the computer contain the danger that the users deal with functions as objects without knowing what they are actually doing. On the whole, the combination of manipulative and reflective aspects and the connected change in standpoint between the conception of process and object turn out to be the basis of effective dealing with functions in mathematical application contexts.

articleTitle: It pays to bluff
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This paper looks at the application of probability theory to a game between two players. It shows how basic techniques such as tree diagrams can be used to demonstrate optimum strategies. In particular, it shows how the art of bluffing can be quantified and how this might be applied to a game of poker.

articleTitle: Recognizing constructs within mathematical modelling
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: There has been much research on specifying frameworks within which the mathematical modelling develops, or assessing such tasks to properly reward student achievement. Little attention has so far been paid to recognizing attainment levels of students at defined stages of a modelling process. In this research we discuss a research tool that has the potential to identify a student's development in mathematical modelling, to gauge the effectiveness of teaching styles adopted and to enhance learning. We report on pilot applications of a questionnaire at two universities in the UK. We discuss the construction and testing of the research instrument and consider implications of the research and directions for further research.

articleTitle: Computer‐based examining in GCE (A level) Decision and Discrete Mathematics
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: The development of Decision and Discrete Mathematics at A level is outlined. The rationale for the subject is explored, as is the argument for a computer‐based examination in an advanced unit. Linear programming is used both as a paradigm and as a unifying concept. Some of the practicalities involved in delivering a computer‐based examination are described.

articleTitle: A computer‐based method for exploring functional relations in geometric figures
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: In this article we propose and exemplify a scheme for linking geometrical and analytical approaches to solving problems expressed in terms of functional relations accessible to upper secondary school pupils. Its purpose is to encourage mathematics educators to link the visual with the analytical as a means to improve the learning of mathematics.

articleTitle: A technology tale: integrating hand‐held CAS into a mathematics curriculum
publicationTitle: Teaching Mathematics and Its Applications: International Journal of the IMA
abstract: This paper recounts the experiences of faculty members as they addressed some of the challenges presented in choosing and integrating a new technology, the TI‐89 hand‐held computer algebra system, into the core mathematics curriculum. Deciding which instrument to choose, preparing and supporting instructors to use the technology, instructing the students to use the technology, affecting the curriculum, affecting classroom assessment, and analysing the effects of the change are related in detail.
